sections.title: God's Sovereign Choice
observations: In this section, Paul addresses the issue of God's sovereignty in choosing individuals for His purposes. He emphasizes that God's election is not based on human merit or effort, but solely on His divine will and purpose.
Paul uses the example of Isaac and Ishmael, as well as Jacob and Esau, to illustrate that God's choice is not determined by lineage or works, but by His sovereign grace.

sections.title: God's Justice and Mercy
observations: Paul anticipates objections regarding God's justice in choosing some and not others. He argues that God has the right to show mercy to whom He wills and to harden whom He wills, as seen in the example of Pharaoh.
This section highlights the tension between divine sovereignty and human responsibility, prompting readers to grapple with the complexities of God's justice.

sections.title: The Remnant of Israel
observations: Paul discusses the concept of a remnant within Israel, indicating that not all of Israel is Israel. He emphasizes that true children of God are those who are of faith, not merely of physical descent.
This section underscores the idea that God's promises are fulfilled in a spiritual sense, and that faith in Christ is the true marker of belonging to God's people.

importantVerses.commentary: Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad, in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of his call.
So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.
And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: 'Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved.'

questions: What does this chapter teach us about the nature of God's sovereignty and human responsibility?
How do we reconcile the idea of God's mercy with His justice in the context of election?
What implications does the concept of a remnant have for our understanding of the church today?
